newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - To bury or not to bury? Russians reconsider Lenin.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - To bury or not to bury? Russians reconsider Lenin.

text.p: Yuri Denisov-Nikolsky has spent much of the last quarter-century helping look after Vladimir Lenin's embalmed corpse, refining techniques he says have preserved the founder of the Soviet state astonishingly well.

"If you took a piece of the corpse's skin and put it under a microscope, a specialist would find it hard to tell it apart from the skin of a person who had only just died," the greying scientist boasted at his Moscow institute.

Not surprisingly, Denisov-Nikolsky wants Lenin's corpse to remain where it is, protected by guards, soft lighting and the carefully regulated air conditioning of the late communist leader's mausoleum on Red Square.
But times have changed. Lenin, who died in 1924 and would have turned 127 on April 22, is again the centre of controversy.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin, a communist turned reformer, has revived proposals to move the father of the Bolshevik revolution from his bullet-proof glass case and bury him next to his mother in St Petersburg.
Communists in the lower house of parliament opposed that as an "act of vandalism".
Meanwhile, calls are gathering momentum to give a ceremonial burial in St Petersburg to Russia's last tsar and his family, murdered by Bolshevik revolutionaries in 1918.
Public debate of the two burials, both rich in symbolism, has revealed a nation still groping to find its identity more than five years after communist rule ended.
"There are people who say Lenin brought our country great evil. There are others who say the opposite. Who is right?" Denisov-Nikolsky, 65, said.
"The discussion reflects the state of our society at a time when opinions are sharply polarised and, in these tough economic times, the debate gets very heated."

In a sign of the emotions, a previously unknown group blew up Moscow's only momument to the last tsar, Nicholas II, earlier this month. It said it acted in protest at the proposals to move Lenin's corpse.
The mausoleum, in front of the red-brick walls of the Kremlin, is a highly visible reminder of the totalitarian era which preceded Russia's efforts to become a democracy.

Some Russians say Lenin's corpse should stay as a warning against the dangers of communist rule. Communists say it should remain as a tribute to his role in history and as a source of hope for them in the future.

"As long as this crystal (Lenin) lives, the Soviet Union, the communist doctrine and the communist red reality can be restored in all its power and beauty," said Alexander Prokhanov, editor of the communist-nationalist newspaper Zavtra.
Scientists such as Denisov-Nikolsky say the corpse should stay where it is to continue a scientific experiment and as a tribute to Soviet, and now Russian, science.

He describes the techniques developed at the Scientific Research Centre of Biologicial Structures where he works as unique. Politicians have been embalmed in other countries but he says Moscow's method is unique and a "commercial secret".
Reasons cited for moving Lenin include demands to give him a Christian burial and to remove a last symbol of another era.
Lenin is the embodiment of communism. Burying him would be seen by many as a final burial of communism itself.
It would almost certainly be welcomed by Yeltsin, who portrayed his re-election campaign last year as a battle to prevent a red tide sweeping back.
Yeltsin beat communist leader Gennady Zyuganov by a big margin in the second round of the election last July, but 30 million people still voted for the challenger.
The communists hold about one third of the seats in the lower house of parliament and, with the support of their parliamentary allies, can block government legislation.
They proposed changes to the constitution earlier this month to bring back the Soviet Union's hammer and sickle emblem but failed to win enough support for the motion to pass.

The communists also suggested replacing the national anthem, a melody from 19th century composer Mikhail Glinka's opera "A life for the Tsar", and reinstating the Soviet anthem introduced by late dictator Josef Stalin.

Such moves reflect deep differences of opinion over what Russia should be and where it is headed, questions that dominated the politics and literature of the last century when society was divided between Westerners and Slavophiles.

Yeltsin says Russians must search for a new ideology after more than seven decades of communist rule and has declared 1997 the Year of Reconciliation and Accord, partly to unite Russians behind one idea and partly to unite them behind him.
"What kind of national ideology is the most important for us?" Yeltsin said in an election rally last July. "One cannot answer this straight away but we must think about it."
St Peterburg's former mayor, Anatoly Sobchak, says the fate of Lenin's corpse is crucial to this debate and it is a question which must be addressed if Russia is to move forward.

"The question of burying Lenin is central from the point of view of changing our mentality. We can find reconciliation and accord only by abandoning the past and thinking seriously about the future," he wrote in the weekly magazine Novoye Vremya.
"The burial of Lenin and of the remains of the tsar and his family will be symbolic of real national reconciliation."
